Whether a change to a request waits for an approval

change_needs_approval.Rd

The one place the rule lives, decided on 2026-10-14. A request belongs to whoever owns it, and the row answers to its owner: a change somebody else had a hand in is carried out only once the owner, or IT, has approved it. The owner is whoever created the row until the round passes it on: since 2026-10-16 the row belongs to the last referent whose change was approved and carried out, log_owner(). So:

Usage

change_needs_approval(
  authors,
  owner,
  sealed = TRUE,
  revocation = FALSE,
  managers = character()
)

Arguments

authors

Who has a hand in the version the round would carry out, as log_pending_authors() answers.

owner

Who owns the row, as log_owner() answers, with "" where it answers NA.

sealed

Whether the row carries the seal of an execution, whose mismatch is what says it changed.

revocation

Whether the change is a revocation and nothing else: the row asks for revoked and log_revocation_only() holds.

managers

Who holds User Rights with Full Access on the project the row names, as the instance reported it this round.

Value

TRUE when the change has to wait for the owner's approval.

Details

  • a change made only by the owner is carried out on the next round, with nobody to ask;

  • a change in which anybody else had a hand waits for the owner, even when the owner edited the row afterwards: a later edit does not say the owner saw the other one, and an approval is the act that does;

  • a change whose authors or whose owner the log cannot establish waits too. "I could not establish who did this" is not "the owner did it".

It holds whether or not the round has applied the row yet. The one difference is what a log naming nobody means. On a row that carries a seal the seal has already moved, so the row did change and nobody is on record for it: it waits. On a row never applied there is no such evidence, and a log that names nobody says nobody changed it.

A revocation is the one exception, decided on 2026-10-15: somebody else's withdrawal of the request does not wait when everybody other than the owner who has a hand in it holds User Rights with Full Access on the project. Taking an access away grants nothing, and whoever manages the users of a project could have removed that person by hand – the rule the scope gate enforces, "nobody does through the channel what they could not do by hand", holds as it is. What counts as a revocation is narrow on purpose, log_revocation_only(): the row now asks for revoked, and what the others wrote is that and nothing else. A withdrawal that also moves the role, the person or the project is a change like any other.

The rights come from the instance, and the round has them only once it has asked it. So the round asks this question twice for a revocation: before talking to the instance, with no managers, which holds it provisionally; and at the gate, with the managers the instance reported, which decides.
